query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A thin, adherent chromium-based diffusion coating on the surface of boride-based components will promote the in situ formation of a stable protective aluminide/oxide layer that inhibits direct molten aluminum attack, thereby reducing the corrosion rate by at least 50% compared to untreated components.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment that currently exhibit inadequate resistance to molten aluminum corrosion.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin, adherent chromium-based diffusion coating onto the boride surface using a controlled surface modification process (e.g., diffusion treatment or sputtering technique).
generation.conditions: Exposure to molten aluminum at typical hot-dip plating temperatures (approximately 660–750°C) for durations representative of industrial processing.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of an in situ protective aluminide/oxide passivation layer at the interface of the chromium-doped region and molten aluminum.
generation.mechanism: The chromium-based diffusion coating modifies the surface chemistry, thereby promoting the formation of a stable, adherent passivation layer that acts as a barrier to direct contact between the molten aluminum and the underlying boride substrate. This passivation layer reduces the wetting and subsequent reactive attack of molten aluminum on the boride phase.
generation.predicted_outcome: At least a 50% reduction in the corrosion rate (assessed via metrics such as weight loss or corrosion penetration depth) compared to untreated boride components under similar molten aluminum exposure conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated boride-based components exposed to molten aluminum under the same high-temperature operational conditions.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected to hold under typical hot-dip aluminum-plating conditions. However, if exposure conditions exceed the normal temperature range or time scales (e.g., significantly higher temperatures or prolonged exposure leading to potential coating degradation), the effectiveness of the passivation layer may diminish.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties include the long-term adhesion stability of the diffusion coating under cyclic thermal stresses and the precise kinetics of the in situ passivation layer formation, which may require further experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of boride-based component samples: one set receiving the chromium-based diffusion coating and a control set remaining unmodified. Subject both sets to molten aluminum exposure at a controlled temperature (e.g., 700°C) for an industrially relevant duration (e.g., 100 hours). Post-exposure, perform quantitative characterization of the corrosion effects (e.g., weight loss measurements, microscopy to determine corrosion penetration depth).
measurements: Corrosion penetration depth via cross-sectional microscopy
Microstructural analysis of the surface passivation layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the chromium-coated samples do not exhibit at least a 50% reduction in corrosion rate (by weight loss or depth of attack) relative to the untreated control under identical exposure conditions, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this work, a reinforced layer on the surface of HEA was successfully synthesized by powder-pack boriding. The microstructure, microhardness, wear resistance, and boriding mechanism were investigated. The following conclusions can be summarized: The microstructure of the surface layer is mainly composed of MB-type boride and M2B-type boride. The original interface of the surface layer is located at the interface between the BL and the diffusion layer, where element B diffuses inward and metal elements diffuse outward. The activation energy and frequency factor of the B element in CoCrFeMnNi HEA are 206.93 kJ/mol and 9.15 × 10−5 m2/s, respectively. Increasing the boronizing duration and temperature resulted in an increase in the BL and diffusion layer thickness. The surface strengthening of CoCrFeMnNi HEA was achieved by the boriding treatment. Its surface microhardness has significantly increased from 3.9 ± 0.1 Gpa to 23.8 ± 1.4 Gpa. The surface layer shows a lower friction coefficient of 0.48 than that of the substrate (0.86). Depending on the wear mechanism, adhesive wear mainly occurs in unboronized samples, and abrasive wear is the main wear mechanism in boronized samples. Th

In addition, to obtain a uniform and stable protective layer, sputtering technology offers a fast deposition rate and a low-cost solution. Although the development of HEA systems has been going on for more than a decade, there are few reports on the deposition of stable protective films on HEA surfaces by conventional reactive sputtering techniques. Many studies have shown that sputter deposition of CrN film on conventional stainless steel is beneficial for its wear and corrosion resistance [,]. The CrN film deposited on the surface of 316 stainless steel has a positive effect on the friction behavior in NaCl solution and high temperature environments until heated to 550 °C []. In the tribo-corrosion test, the CrN coating layer can also remain relatively stable during the ball-on-plate sliding under various applied potentials []. As stainless steels are similar to CoCrNi-based MEAs in terms of their single FCC structure and lattice constant, this study attempts to sputter CrN film with a Cr buffer layer on the surface of CoCrNiSi0.3 MEA and discusses in detail the improvement of corrosion and wear resistance of CoCrNiSi0.3 MEA by sputtering CrN film.

frame.system: Boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment that are exposed to molten aluminum at high temperature.
frame.goal: Improve the resistance of the components to corrosion by molten aluminum.
frame.limitation: Current boride surfaces suffer from inadequate corrosion resistance when directly exposed to molten aluminum, likely due to wetting and reactive attack of the molten metal on the boride phase.
constraints: The intervention must be a single, well-defined modification
Hypothesis must predict measurable improvement relative to a baseline (unmodified boride components)
The hypothesis should specify the operational conditions (e.g., temperature, molten aluminum exposure) under which the improvement is expected
It must include a controlled experimental design that could falsify the prediction
frame.regime: High-temperature environment wherein the component is exposed to molten aluminum (likely in the range typical for hot-dip plating, e.g., 660–750°C) during processing or service.
prior_attempts: Use of undoped or untreated boride-based materials that have shown insufficient corrosion resistance under molten aluminum exposure
frame.understanding: There is an incomplete understanding of how an engineered surface modification can inhibit the direct reaction between molten aluminum and the boride phase, leading to degradation of the component.
frame.method: The hypothesis proposes modifying the surface chemistry by introducing a thin, adherent, and chemically inert passivation layer (for example, via surface deposition or diffusion doping with a small amount of chromium or silicon) that promotes the formation of a stable, protective aluminide or oxide scale. This scale is expected to prevent the direct contact and reaction between the aggressive molten aluminum and the underlying boride substrate. The hypothesis predicts that components treated with this single intervention will exhibit at least a 50% reduction in corrosion rate compared to untreated controls when subjected to the same molten aluminum immersion tests. The improvement should remain effective within the typical operational temperature range of hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment. Supporting evidence comes from studies in high-temperature corrosion where surface alloying or coating with chromium or silicon has been shown to form stable protective scales that limit metal–molten metal interactions. A controlled experiment would involve preparing two sets of boride-based samples (one with the surface intervention and one as a control), then subjecting them to identical molten aluminum immersion tests at controlled temperatures and durations, followed by quantitative measurement of corrosion depth or weight loss to assess the improvement. Failure of the treated sample to meet the predicted reduction in corrosion rate would falsify the hypothesis.

decision.trend: Earlier work in high‐temperature corrosion environments has largely focused on modifying bulk alloy compositions to minimize element dissolution in aggressive media (e.g., molten FLiBe salts or simulated reactor water). More recently, researchers have shifted toward surface modification techniques to tailor the interfacial chemistry. For example, studies such as PMC10221107 used powder‐pack boriding on high-entropy alloys to form hard, boride-rich layers that improved wear and, in some cases, corrosion performance. Although these methods enhanced surface properties, none directly addressed the specific problem of molten aluminum wetting and reaction that degrades boride phases.
decision.unsolved: The core challenge remains how to inhibit the direct contact and reactive attack between molten aluminum and the boride substrate under hot-dip aluminum-plating conditions. While surface treatments like boriding have been beneficial in other contexts, a single, targeted intervention that forms a stable passivation layer to block molten aluminum from attacking the boride phase has not yet been established.
decision.lever: Introduce a thin, adherent chromium-based (or similarly effective silicon-based) diffusion coating on the boride surface to promote the in situ formation of a stable protective aluminide/oxide passivation layer.
decision.why: This approach logically extends the trend of utilizing surface modifications to control high-temperature interactions. By applying a controlled diffusion layer, the interface can be engineered to resist molten aluminum wetting and reaction, thereby reducing the corrosion rate by the predicted 50% compared to untreated boride components. This specific surface intervention directly addresses the unsolved issue highlighted in previous research and aligns with the operational conditions of hot-dip aluminum plating.
